issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, sexual-violence comments as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless the index event also involved sexual assault or closely related content; nothing else in the profile supports that connection.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal of betrayal by a trusted person is difficult to fit with terrorism as the trauma type unless there was a clear interpersonal betrayal component; the rest of the selected items describe loss of control, helplessness, avoidance, dissociation, and substance use rather than interpersonal betrayal.

vignette: At thirty-seven, Arjun had built a quiet, predictable life as a clinical psychologist and a devoted husband, but the terrorism bombing at a downtown transit hub six months ago fractured that foundation. He had been standing near the central kiosk when the initial detonation collapsed the ceiling grid, pinning him beneath twisted rebar and shattered glass. For nearly two minutes, he was completely immobilized, watching panic spread through the crowd while his own limbs refused to respond to his commands. When emergency crews finally dragged him free, the area was plunged into a heavy, smoke-choked dark, and the sharp, rhythmic crack of automatic gunfire echoed from adjacent buildings, overlapping the sirens. Arjun was certain he would not survive the night. The event carved a permanent fissure in his nervous system; the combination of physical paralysis, the sudden swallowing of light, and the staccato gunfire became an inextricable knot of terror that would dictate his life long after the dust settled. The trauma's aftershocks arrived first as visceral intrusions. When Arjun woke at 3 a.m., the familiar quiet of his bedroom suddenly felt like a suffocating void, and any distant thump of a passing car triggered a full-body jolt, his breath catching as the phantom sounds of gunfire replaced the hum of his refrigerator. He was certain that disaster could strike without warning, that his safety was an illusion. The person he had become in the weeks following the blast felt like a stranger; he watched himself flinch at sudden movements and struggle to recognize his own reflection in the mirror. What frightened him most was the conviction that the world had fundamentally shifted into a place where violence was omnipresent and his own hands were utterly powerless to stop it. As a psychologist managing a busy downtown practice, Arjun's own office became the stage where his symptoms played out with brutal clarity. During his regular late-night charting hours, when the building's climate control clicked off and the room descended into a quiet gloom, the sudden absence of ambient noise felt like a physical trap. The moment the overhead fluorescent bulb flickered and the distant groan of a delivery truck echoed up the stairwell, his shoulders locked and his breath shallowed. These sensory alarms instantly drove him to abandon his work. He would pour a heavy measure of scotch, leave the clinic door shut against the night, and deliberately drift into a detached, dreamlike fugue. To manage the crushing pressure, he began systematically avoiding every nonessential deadline, canceling peer consultations, and convincing himself that chemical numbness was the only viable shield against the day. Over the following months, the cycle tightened into a rigid architecture of survival. His deep-seated belief that he could not prevent catastrophe only made him more reliant on his escape routes, as he viewed coping as a futile exercise and his changed identity as a permanent sentence. Consequently, he withdrew from every demanding task, leaning harder into isolation and intoxication. Yet each episode of avoidance only confirmed his worst fears; by withdrawing, he starved himself of disconfirming evidence, leaving his conviction of helplessness and global threat unchallenged and increasingly absolute. The very strategies meant to protect him began to lower his threshold for fear, so that minor stressors now masqueraded as existential threats, and the lingering effects of his nightly drinks left him mentally foggy, making him even more susceptible to the jarring intrusions of memory and sound when they inevitably returned. The unraveling reached its peak during a routine group session when a patient's sudden cough echoed through the room, sending Arjun into a silent panic that nearly caused him to abandon his practice entirely. He had come to realize that his professional competence and his marriage were fraying under the weight of his own survival tactics. He finally sat in my office not because he believed he could simply "fix" himself, but because he was terrified of becoming completely invisible to his wife and his colleagues. He was hoping to find a way to sit with the discomfort without fleeing, even if he was most afraid that the world was still waiting for the next strike and his mind would never again feel like his own.
